grammar.title: Superlativos + present perfect · the first time
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Superlativo + present perfect + ever** → a maior/melhor/pior experiência **até agora**:
- "It's **the most inspiring** talk I**'ve ever seen**."
- "She's **the kindest** person I**'ve ever met**."
- "That's **the hardest** thing I**'ve ever done**."
(o **that/who** antes do sujeito pode ser omitido: "the best book (that) I've ever read")

**It's the first/second/only time + present perfect** → experiência vivida agora:
- "**It's the first time** I**'ve spoken** in public."
- "**This is the third time** I**'ve visited** Lisbon."

⚠️ No **passado**, a estrutura muda para **past perfect**: "**It was the first time** I**'d ever seen** snow." (No A2/B1 você viu o past perfect — aqui ele volta!)

**Never... before** → também expressa primeira vez: "I**'ve never** worked with such a diverse team **before**."

**Expressões de aprendizado:**
- "I**'ve learned** (how) **to** + verbo": "I've learned to listen more."
- "I**'ve learned that** + frase": "I've learned that everyone communicates differently."
- "X **has taught me to/that**...": "My brother has taught me to be patient."

rows: It's the best decision I've ever made.
It's the first time + present perfect
It's the first time I've tried this.
It was the first time + past perfect
It was the first time I'd flown alone.
I've never felt so welcome before.
Life has taught me that nothing is permanent.

grammar.tip_pt: Ao falar de deficiência, prefira linguagem que a própria comunidade usa. Muitos preferem **"person with a disability"** (person-first) e muitos autistas preferem **"autistic person"** (identity-first). Na dúvida, pergunte ou siga como a pessoa se descreve.

common_mistakes.why_pt: Superlativo + experiência até agora = present perfect (padrão britânico e de provas).

common_mistakes.wrong: It's the first time I come here.

common_mistakes.wrong: It was the first time I've seen snow.
common_mistakes.right: It was the first time I'd seen snow.
common_mistakes.why_pt: No passado (It was), use past perfect.

pronunciation.tip_pt: **I've ever** se junta: "**áivéver**". Na frase, a força vai no superlativo e no particípio: "the **BEST** book I've ever **READ**". **Eye-opening** = "ÁI-ôupenin".

lines.speaker: HR Manager
lines.en: Three years ago, we started a program to hire more neurodivergent people — for example, autistic people and people with ADHD or dyslexia. It's been the best decision we've ever made. We changed our interviews: instead of asking abstract questions, we let candidates show their skills with practical tasks. We created quiet rooms and allowed flexible hours. The results? Our data team, which now includes several neurodivergent analysts, has found errors that nobody had noticed for years. But the biggest change has been cultural. Everyone has learned to communicate more clearly — and that has helped all of us.

reading.title: Different minds at work
reading.text: For a long time, many workplaces were designed for one type of brain. Job interviews rewarded people who were good at small talk and eye contact, open-plan offices were full of noise, and instructions were often vague. As a result, many talented neurodivergent people — including autistic people and people with ADHD or dyslexia — struggled to find or keep jobs. In recent years, some large companies have started neurodiversity hiring programs. Instead of traditional interviews, candidates might spend a few days solving real problems, and managers receive training on how to give clear, direct feedback. Several of these companies report that neurodivergent employees bring valuable strengths, such as pattern recognition, attention to detail, creative problem-solving and deep focus. Advocates point out, however, that the goal shouldn't only be productivity. "Inclusion isn't about finding hidden superpowers," one autistic activist explains. "It's about accepting that people think differently — and that's normal."

questions.q: Why did many neurodivergent people struggle at work?
questions.answer: Workplaces were designed for one type of brain (small talk, noise, vague instructions).

questions.q: How are some hiring programs different?
questions.answer: Candidates solve real problems for a few days; managers learn to give clear feedback.

questions.q: What strengths are mentioned?
questions.answer: Pattern recognition, attention to detail, creative problem-solving and deep focus.

questions.q: What do advocates say the goal should be?

writing.model: The person who has changed the way I see the world the most is my grandfather, Seu João. He grew up on a farm in Bahia and left school when he was ten, but he's the wisest person I've ever met. When I was a teenager, I thought success meant money and a big title. My grandfather taught me a different lesson. Every morning, he would share his coffee with the street sweepers and ask about their families. "Everyone has something to teach you," he used to say. It was the first time I'd seen so many different people in one room — doctors, farmers, children, neighbors — all there because he had been kind to them. grammar.title: Previsões com graus de certeza
grammar.explanation_pt:
No B1+, em vez de usar só **will**, mostre **o quanto você tem certeza**:

**100% →** will definitely / be bound to (com certeza vai) / certainly will
"Electric cars **will definitely** become cheaper." / "There**'s bound to** be traffic."

**~80% →** will probably / be likely to + verbo
"Most new cars **will probably** be electric by 2035." / "Prices **are likely to** fall."

**~50% →** may / might / could + verbo (talvez)
"Flying taxis **might** be available in some cities." / "It **could** take decades."

**~20% →** probably won't / be unlikely to / I doubt (that)...
"People **probably won't** stop driving completely." / "It's **unlikely to** happen soon."

**0% →** definitely won't / there's no way...
"Cars **definitely won't** disappear by 2030."

**Posição dos advérbios:**
- afirmativa: **will + advérbio** → "It **will probably** rain."
- negativa: **advérbio + won't** → "It **probably won't** rain." (❌ "It won't probably")

**Futuro contínuo e perfeito (reconhecimento):**
- "In 2040, we**'ll be traveling** in autonomous cars." (ação em andamento num momento futuro)
- "By 2035, many countries **will have banned** new gasoline cars." (concluído até um ponto futuro)

rows: EVs are likely to get cheaper.

examples.en: Electric buses are likely to replace diesel buses in most big cities.
examples.pt: Ônibus elétricos provavelmente vão substituir os ônibus a diesel na maioria das cidades grandes.

examples.en: Self-driving cars might be safer, but people probably won't trust them for a while.

examples.en: By 2040, many cities will have closed their centers to private cars.

grammar.tip_pt: **Be likely to** é muito usado em notícias e relatórios: "The new law **is likely to** affect millions of drivers." É uma ótima forma de soar mais sofisticado do que "will probably".

common_mistakes.why_pt: Na negativa, o advérbio vem antes de won't.

common_mistakes.wrong: Maybe flying cars will might exist.
common_mistakes.right: Flying cars might exist. / Maybe flying cars will exist.

pronunciation.tip_pt: Na fala rápida, **probably** vira "**PRÓB-li**" (quase duas sílabas) e **definitely** vira "**DÉF-net-li**". **Likely** = "LÁIK-li". A força está sempre no começo dessas palavras.

listening.title: Transport predictions
listening.context_pt: Uma especialista em mobilidade urbana faz previsões para os próximos 20 anos.

lines.speaker: Expert
lines.en: Let me make a few predictions. First, electric vehicles will definitely dominate new car sales in many countries — that's already happening. Second, cities are likely to invest more in bikes, e-scooters and public transport, because they're cheaper and take up less space. Third, self-driving cars might become common on highways, but I doubt we'll see many in chaotic city centers soon — the technology still struggles with unpredictable situations. And flying taxis? They could appear in a few rich cities, but they're unlikely to become a normal way to commute. Most people will still be taking the bus in 2045 — just a cleaner, quieter bus.

reading.title: The 15-minute city
reading.text: What if everything you needed — work, school, shops, a doctor, a park — was within a 15-minute walk or bike ride from your home? That's the idea behind the "15-minute city", a concept developed by the urbanist Carlos Moreno and adopted by Paris and other cities around the world. Supporters argue that it's likely to reduce traffic, pollution and stress, while making neighborhoods more lively and social. In Paris, the city has created hundreds of kilometers of new bike lanes and turned some streets around schools into car-free zones. Critics, however, say the idea may not work in places with low population density, where shops and jobs are far apart. Others worry that it could increase housing prices in well-designed neighborhoods, pushing poorer residents out. Some online conspiracy theories have even claimed, without evidence, that 15-minute cities are a plan to restrict people's freedom of movement. The debate is bound to continue — but as cities grow and the climate crisis worsens, many planners believe that shorter, greener journeys are the future.

writing.model:
Transport in Curitiba in 2045

Curitiba has always been a pioneer in public transport, so its future is likely to be exciting. First, the city's famous bus rapid transit system will definitely continue, but the buses are bound to be fully electric and much quieter. Second, the number of bike lanes is likely to double, because more young people prefer cycling to driving. Self-driving cars might become common on highways around the city, but I doubt they will be popular in the busy center, where pedestrians and cyclists make traffic unpredictable. Flying taxis could appear for business travelers, but they're unlikely to be affordable for most people. On the other hand, private cars probably won't disappear completely, especially for families in the suburbs. In my opinion, the biggest change will be cultural: by 2045, many residents will have stopped seeing the car as a symbol of status, and the city will probably be greener, quieter and more pleasant to live in.

culture_note.title: "Transport" ou "transportation"?

grammar.title: Modals of deduction: present and past
grammar.explanation_pt:
Usamos **modais de dedução** para dizer o que achamos que **é verdade** com base em evidências.

**PRESENTE — modal + verbo base (ou be + -ing):**
- **must** = tenho quase certeza que **sim**: "You've been working for 12 hours. You **must be** tired."
- **might / may / could** = **talvez**: "He's not answering. He **might be** in a meeting."
- **can't** = tenho quase certeza que **não**: "That **can't be** Ana. She's in Japan."
⚠️ O oposto de **must** (dedução) é **can't**, não "mustn't" (mustn't = proibição).

**PASSADO — modal + have + particípio:**
- **must have** + particípio = com certeza aconteceu: "The streets are wet. It **must have rained**."
- **might / may / could have** + particípio = talvez tenha acontecido: "She's late. She **might have missed** the bus."
- **can't / couldn't have** + particípio = com certeza **não** aconteceu: "He **can't have stolen** the money — he was with me all night."

**Para ação em andamento:**
- presente: "She **must be working** late."
- passado: "They **must have been sleeping** when the alarm went off."

Na fala, **must have** = "**mâstav**", **might have** = "**máitav**", **can't have** = "**kéntav**".

rows: must have been / must have worked

listening.title: Innovation podcast: simple solutions
listening.context_pt: Um podcast sobre invenções simples que resolvem grandes problemas.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.en: Today, let's talk about simple inventions that might change millions of lives. Take the solar-powered lamp, for example. In places without electricity, families often use kerosene lamps, which are expensive and dangerous. A cheap solar lamp could save money and prevent fires. Or consider low-cost water filters made from clay and sawdust. The inventors must have asked themselves: what materials do local people already have? That's the secret. The best solutions often aren't the most high-tech ones. They're the ones that people can afford, repair and actually use. So the next time you face a problem, ask yourself: could the answer be simpler than I think?

reading.title: The mystery of the Voynich manuscript
reading.text: In 1912, a book dealer named Wilfrid Voynich bought a strange manuscript from a collection in Italy. The book, which is now kept at Yale University, has about 240 pages full of drawings of unknown plants, astronomical diagrams and women bathing in green pools. But the strangest thing is the text: it's written in an alphabet that nobody has ever been able to read. Carbon dating has shown that the parchment must have been made in the early 15th century. So who wrote it, and why? Some researchers believe it might be written in a lost natural language. Others think it could be a code designed to hide secret medical or alchemical knowledge. Some skeptics argue that it can't contain real meaning at all: it might have been a clever hoax, created to sell to a rich collector. Over the years, linguists, cryptographers and even AI programs have tried to decode it, and several people have claimed to have solved the mystery — but none of their solutions has been widely accepted. For now, the Voynich manuscript remains one of the most famous unsolved puzzles in the world.

writing.model:
Case report: The empty office

On Monday morning, employees at a design studio in Belo Horizonte found something strange. All the plants in the office had been moved to the meeting room, every chair was facing the window, and there was a birthday cake on the table with no name on it. Nobody remembered ordering it.

There are several possible explanations. First, the cleaning team might have moved the plants to clean the floor, but this can't explain the cake. Second, someone must have had a key, because the door wasn't damaged. The manager, who was the only person in the office on Sunday, could have organized a surprise for somebody — but he says he didn't. Finally, the chairs facing the window are a clue: someone might have been planning a photo session.

The truth? On Tuesday, the receptionist admitted that she had organized a surprise party for her colleague's birthday — but she had got the date wrong. It must have been an awkward Monday!

grammar.title: Linguagem de telefone e mensagens
grammar.explanation_pt:
Ao telefone, a linguagem é bem **fixa** — aprenda em **blocos**:

**1. Identificar-se:** em inglês, diga **"This is..."** (não "I am..."): "Hello, **this is** Pedro from Alfa Bank." / Para perguntar quem fala: "**Who's calling, please?**" / "**May I ask who's calling?**"

**2. Pedir para falar com alguém:** "**Could I speak to**...?" / "**I'm calling about**..." / "**I'm returning** Ms. Lee's **call**."

**3. Pedidos educados:** **will / would / could** — "**Could you** ask her to call me back?" / "**Would you** mind spelling that?"

**4. Ofertas com will (decisão na hora):** "**I'll** put you through." / "**I'll** tell him you called." / "**I'll** call back later."

**5. Passar recados (reported requests — introdução):**
- Ela disse: "Call me back." → **She asked you to call her back.**
- Ele disse: "I'll be late." → **He said (that) he'd be late.**
(Você vai aprofundar o reported speech no Módulo 6!)

**6. Estrutura de uma boa mensagem de voz:**
1. Cumprimento + **quem é** (nome + empresa)
2. **Hora/data** da ligação
3. **Motivo** da ligação
4. **Ação** pedida ("Could you call me back...?")
5. **Número** — falado **devagar**, de preferência **duas vezes**
6. Despedida

reading.title: Why we hate phone calls
reading.text: For many young professionals, an unexpected phone call feels almost like an emergency. Surveys in the UK and the US have found that a large number of people under 35 avoid answering calls from unknown numbers, and many feel anxious when they have to make a call. Some even rehearse what they're going to say before dialing. Why? Researchers point to several reasons. Text messages and emails give us time to think and edit; phone calls happen in real time, with no chance to delete a mistake. Calls can also feel intrusive: they interrupt whatever you're doing. And for people speaking a second language, the lack of facial expressions and gestures makes understanding much harder. However, many managers say that phone calls are still the fastest way to solve complex problems and build relationships. A five-minute call can save twenty emails. The solution? Practice. Experts suggest preparing a few key phrases, keeping a notepad ready and remembering that it's completely normal to say: "Sorry, could you repeat that?"

culture_note.title: Ligar sem avisar?
culture_note.text_pt: Em muitos ambientes profissionais de língua inglesa, ligar sem avisar é cada vez menos comum. É educado mandar uma mensagem antes: **"Do you have five minutes for a quick call?"** ou **"Can I give you a ring?"** (UK). E no WhatsApp, áudios longos de trabalho podem ser malvistos — prefira texto ou uma chamada marcada.

summary_pt: Ao telefone: This is... (não I am).
Could I speak to...? / I'll put you through / Can I take a message?
Mensagem de voz: quem → quando → motivo → ação → número (2x).
Recados: She asked me to... / He said (that)...

review.intro_pt: Revise superlativos com present perfect, previsões, modais de dedução e linguagem de telefone.

items.prompt: It's the most beautiful place I ___.
It was the first time I ___ abroad.
Prices ___ rise next year.
That ___ be Ana. She's in Tokyo.
Hello, ___ Pedro from Alfa Bank.
It ___ (probably / not) rain tomorrow.
The streets are wet. It ___ (must / rain) last night.
She ___ (ask) me to call her back.
É o melhor conselho que já recebi.
items.answer: It's the best advice I've ever received.

items.prompt: Ele deve ter esquecido.
Infelizmente ela está numa reunião. Posso anotar um recado?
items.answer: I'm afraid she's in a meeting. Can I take a message?
That was a turning point in my life.
They might have missed the train.

items.prompt: It's the first time I visit Paris.
items.answer: It's the first time I've visited Paris.

items.prompt: It won't probably work.
She must forgot the keys.
items.answer: She must have forgotten the keys.

review.speaking_pt: Grave um áudio de 3 minutos em dois momentos: (1) conte a experiência mais marcante da sua vida e o que aprendeu com ela; (2) faça três previsões sobre como será sua vida em 2040, cada uma com um grau de certeza diferente.
speaking_questions: What's the most important lesson you've ever learned?
What will definitely change in your life in the next ten years?
What might happen that would surprise you?
Think of a mystery in your life. What might have happened?
How comfortable are you making phone calls in English now?
review.project_pt: **Future lab:** em grupo, escolham um problema real da cidade (trânsito, enchentes, acessibilidade...) e criem uma "invenção" que poderia resolvê-lo. Apresentem: o problema, o que pode tê-lo causado (modais de dedução), a solução e previsões sobre o impacto (likely to / might / will definitely). Bônus: gravem uma mensagem de voz "vendendo" a ideia a um investidor.
